$comment: Why two published packages describe one thing differently, read by scripts/check_label_agreement.py. It sits beside registry.json rather than inside a package because no single descriptor can own a statement about two of them. EACH ENTRY PINS THE VALUES IT EXCUSES, and that is the whole mechanism: a reason closes ONE difference between THESE values, so a package moving one of them makes the entry stop matching, the check exits 1 as a stale reason, and the difference is reported again. An entry that named only the label would be a standing licence to disagree about it forever, which is silencing the check with extra steps. An entry with no `reason` sentence is refused outright. Nothing here is written by a script — a check that can write its own exemptions can be silenced by running it. Differences absent from this file are OPEN: the check prints them on every run with the entry that would close them, and does not fail, because two packages may legitimately differ where their populations differ and no check can know which. `corrections` is the OPPOSITE list and it closes nothing. A reason says a difference is legitimate; a correction says it is a defect, names the side that is wrong, the value it must become and the act that lands the fix — and the difference goes on being reported and `--strict` goes on failing on it. That asymmetry is the whole mechanism: a correction that closed a difference would be a reason with a different word on it, and a bug excused by a sentence. What it buys is that the answer is written where the check can hold it to the packages: each entry pins a declaration by a `pointer` addressed by NAME rather than by index, so it reddens when the declaration moves AND when the fix arrives, and it can be deleted only by the thing being true. It reaches declarations the comparison never sees — a description, a join's cardinality — because the instances this file has to account for do not all live in the space between two constraints. A CORRECTION IS BLOCKED ON AN ACT THIS REPOSITORY CANNOT MAKE ALONE: a descriptor is stamped into the Parquet footer of the object it describes and declares that object's sha256, so changing a published declaration is a republish and not an edit, and a surface in another repository is changed there. That is why a verdict is recorded rather than applied. An empty `corrections` list means no verdict is outstanding.

reasons.reason: The GLEIF register types these elements differently and this label is coarser than that distinction. LEI-CDF v3.1 types `country` as CountryCodeType, a two-letter code and nothing else, and `jurisdiction` as JurisdictionCodeType, a union of CountryCodeType and RegionCodeType which admits country-hyphen-subdivision (US-DE, AE-SH). `edgar_gleif.jurisdiction` is that same `jurisdiction` element carried through the join, declared `geography.location.country_code` in its package's nominations.finetype.json because no label names the union, and it declares the same union pattern as `gleif.jurisdiction`. Each pattern is the shape its own element is typed to, the descriptions in both descriptors say so, and making `country` agree with the two `jurisdiction` columns would mean one of them lying about the register it came from. Note the direction for a reader validating all three: every value `country` admits, both `jurisdiction` columns admit too.

The populations differ and the patterns are each true of their own. `edgar` carries a ticker for every security in the SEC company-tickers file; `edgar_gleif` carries only the subset that resolved to an LEI. The four-letter-plus-period form occurs in the EDGAR column and `edgar.ticker` is widened to admit it — its `x-finetype-pattern-fit` records the widening against finetype's canonical pattern — while the crosswalk snapshot contains no such value and declares the canonical pattern unwidened. So `edgar`'s pattern is the union of the two: a validation routine written against it passes both datasets, and one written against `edgar_gleif`'s narrower pattern fails on EDGAR rows. That asymmetry is the thing worth knowing, and it is why this is recorded rather than closed by widening `edgar_gleif` — a pattern wider than its own column would be less true of the bytes it describes, and changing it would need a republish of the object whose footer carries this descriptor.

Two register elements under one label, each with its own bounds. `edgar.company_name` and `edgar_gleif.company_name` are the SEC display name of a registrant, declared `representation.text.entity_name` in each package's nominations.finetype.json, and they carry that label's own bounds of 2 to 200 characters, which the descriptor check holds every value in both columns to. `gleif.legal_name` and `edgar_gleif.legal_name` are the GLEIF register's legal-name element, which LEI-CDF v3.1 types as Tokenized500Type, 1 to 500 characters; single-character and longer-than-200-character names are genuinely registered, so those two columns carry the register's bounds rather than the label's, and both descriptors say so. The direction for a reader validating all four: the register's bounds admit every company name, and the label's bounds would refuse real register names. In fda/ndc, `product_type` is the FDA's product type and carries the label's bounds; `labeler_name`, `brand_name` and `brand_name_suffix` are names labelers submit, which run to one character (a suffix such as R) and past 200 (a brand name of 367 characters), so they declare 1 to 256, 1 to 512 and 1 to 256.

Each pattern and length is the shape its own column holds. `hts.code` and `schedule_b.code` are the keys of two code lists, digits only, at every level of their outline: 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 digits in usitc/hts, and 2, 4, 6 and 10 in census/schedule_b, which has no eight-digit level. Each declares exactly those lengths, bounded 2 to 10. The `code_display` beside each is the code as its issuer prints it, dotted from the subheading down (0101.21.00 in the HTS, 0101.21.0000 in Schedule B), so it carries finetype's canonical `geography.transportation.hs_code` pattern, which admits the dotted and undotted 6, 8 and 10-digit forms, widened by `^[0-9]{2}$|^[0-9]{4}$` for the chapter and heading rows, and no length bounds. `hts.rate_from_code` names the line a row takes its duty rates from, and only a subheading, tariff line or statistical line prints rates, so it is 6, 8 or 10 digits, bounded 6 to 10. The direction for a reader validating them together: the `code_display` pattern admits every value of the other three columns, and each `code` pattern refuses the dotted forms and the lengths its own list does not have.

The populations differ. `naics.code` is the NAICS 2022 list itself, codes of 2 to 6 digits and the three sector ranges (31-33, 44-45, 48-49), and carries the label's canonical pattern with no length bounds. `schedule_b.naics` is the industry code Census prints on each Schedule B commodity line, always six characters, four digits then two digits or X, which is the shape the census/schedule_b drift contract enforces; it is declared so, with a fixed length of 6. Not every code Census prints has the label's canonical shape: 223 of the 9,779 lines fall outside it, the 62 that end in X (33641X, 1121XX) and the 161 that carry Census's own 930000 (142) or 990000 (19). That is a different count from the join's. 315 lines name no NAICS 2022 code, as the `x-joins` in census/schedule_b measures, because 910000 (92 lines) has the canonical shape but is not in the list. Narrowing `schedule_b.naics` to NAICS's pattern would refuse codes Census really prints, and widening `naics.code` would make it less true of the list it is. A reader should take the pattern difference as one of shape and the join's coverage as one of membership.

One label, two storage choices, each true of its column. `gleif.entity_status` is the register's status element stored as text, LEI-CDF v3.1's three terms ACTIVE, INACTIVE and the four-character string NULL, every row carrying one, so it declares that enum and `required`. `schedule_b.agricultural` is a native Parquet BOOLEAN made from Census's USDA field: it needs no enum, since the type admits only true and false, and it is NULL on the chapter, heading and subheading rows, which print no USDA field, so it is not required. Typing the boolean as text to match would lose its type, and an enum or `required` on it would be false of its own rows. `ndc.sample` in fda/ndc is the same kind of column as `schedule_b.agricultural`: a native BOOLEAN, NULL on the labeler and product rows, which are not packages, so it declares no enum and is not required.

The label names a shape, not a scheme, and each of these columns is its own identifier scheme with its own bounds. `gleif.legal_form` is an ISO 20275 Entity Legal Form code, always four letters or digits, so its length is fixed at 4. In census/schedule_b, `sitc` is an SITC Revision 4 code of five characters, three digits then two digits or X (792XX), fixed at 5, and `unit_1` and `unit_2` are Census's unit-of-quantity abbreviations, one to three uppercase letters or digits (X, KG, M2, DOZ), bounded 1 to 3. The release columns are names of one snapshot each, not codes from a list with a published length: `hts.release` and `schedule_b.hts_release` are USITC's revision name (2026HTSRev22), and `schedule_b.release` is Census's year folder and file date (2026/2026-07-27). So they carry the label's canonical pattern and no length bounds, widened for `schedule_b.release`'s date as its `x-finetype-pattern-fit` records. In cms/hcpcs, `betos` is CMS's Berenson-Eggers Type of Service category, a letter, a digit and an optional letter (Z2, O1E), bounded 2 to 3, and `release` is CMS's quarter and file date (2026-10/2026-09-23), always 18 characters, which it declares exactly. A shared pattern or length would be false of all but one scheme. In fda/ndc, `release` is openFDA's last-updated date (2026-10-30), always 10 characters, which it declares exactly; `product_id` is the FDA's listing identifier, a product NDC and a labeling document's UUID joined with an underscore, of no fixed length, so it carries the label's canonical pattern; and `application_number` is the application or monograph a product is marketed under (NDA217806, M017, 333G(a)(9)), which declares no pattern because monograph citations carry brackets the canonical pattern refuses.

The same label on codes of different lengths, stored two ways. `edgar.cik` is stored as an integer, unpadded, and its description says the decimal rendering is the CIK, so no string pattern or length applies to it. The others are text because their leading zeros are part of the code, and each declares its own length. `hts.parent_code` and `schedule_b.parent_code` are a parent's code, 2 to 8 digits in usitc/hts and 2 to 6 in census/schedule_b, which has no eight-digit level. `schedule_b.end_use` is Census's five-digit end-use code (00000 to 60010) and `schedule_b.hitech` its two-digit high-technology code (00 to 10), each fixed at its length. Stored as integers, 01 would become 1 and no longer join to `code`, and a shared length would be false of all but one of them. `ndc.parent_code` is a parent's code in fda/ndc: a labeler's five digits or a product's nine, the prefixes of the eleven-digit NDC.

The same label inferred on columns of different kinds. `edgar_gleif.key` is text because it carries two SEC schemes in one column, Central Index Keys in decimal digits and fund series identifiers with a letter prefix (S…, CEF…), so it declares the pattern and lengths of that union, as its `x-finetype-pattern-fit` records. `hts.depth`, `hts.indent` and `schedule_b.depth` are true integers, a level's position in the outline (0 to 4) and USITC's printed indent (0 to 11), typed as integers with no string constraints. `hcpcs.depth` is the same integer as the other depths, always 0 in a one-level list. Making either side agree would mean typing the integers as text or the mixed key as a number. `ndc.depth` is the same integer (0 to 2), and `ndc.listing_count` a count of the FDA's listings for a product.

A shared column name, not a shared concept. Every Meridian code list names its key column `code` (with `level`, `depth`, `parent_code` and `description` beside it), so a reader can walk any of them the same way. In census/naics_2022 that key is a NAICS code; in usitc/hts and census/schedule_b it is an HS-based tariff or export code. In cms/hcpcs it is a HCPCS Level II code, labelled `identity.medical.hcpcs`. Each package's label is right for its own code system, and making them agree would mislabel one of them. In fda/ndc it is a National Drug Code, labelled `identity.medical.ndc`.

One label on columns that are not one concept: `representation.text.word` is what finetype infers for any short token. Where the issuer's own documentation defines the column's values as a closed set, cms/hcpcs declares that set as an enum, as its data holds it: `level` is always 'code'; `text_source` is cms or cms_cpt_redacted; `action_code`, `coverage_code`, `multiple_pricing_indicator` and `asc_payment_group` take the codes CMS's HCPCS record layout lists for each. Each of those enums is true of its own column and of no other, so it declares no length or pattern beside it. The other columns, in other packages, carry the label's canonical token pattern and its 1 to 100 length; whether any of them should declare its own closed set is a question for its own package, and making cms/hcpcs agree with them would loosen six declarations that CMS's record layout or this Protocol fixes. fda/ndc declares closed sets the same way: `level` is labeler, product or package; `text_source` is always fda; and `dea_schedule` is one of the Drug Enforcement Administration's five schedules, CI to CV. Its `marketing_category` is the FDA's marketing category, a list the FDA can extend between fortnightly refreshes, so it carries the label's length and no enum.

Each of those enums is true of its own column and of no other, so it declares no length or pattern beside it. The other columns, in other packages, carry the label's canonical token pattern and its 1 to 100 length; whether any of them should declare its own closed set is a question for its own package, and making cms/hcpcs agree with them would loosen six declarations that CMS's record layout or this Protocol fixes. fda/ndc declares closed sets the same way: `level` is labeler, product or package; `text_source` is always fda; and `dea_schedule` is one of the Drug Enforcement Administration's five schedules, CI to CV. Its `marketing_category` is the FDA's marketing category, a list the FDA can extend between fortnightly refreshes, so it carries the label's length and no enum.

The same shared column name as `code`, carrying each code list's own code system as its issuer prints it: HS-based codes, dotted, in usitc/hts and census/schedule_b, and HCPCS Level II codes in cms/hcpcs, which CMS prints with no punctuation. Each label is right for its own code system, and making them agree would mislabel one of them. In fda/ndc it is the FDA's hyphenated National Drug Code, labelled `identity.medical.ndc`.

cms/hcpcs is a one-level list, so its `parent_code` is NULL on every row and finetype has no value to infer a label from; it is `unknown`. In usitc/hts and census/schedule_b `parent_code` holds the digits-only code one level up. Nominating a label for a column with no values would state a shape no row shows. In fda/ndc it holds the labeler's five digits or the product's nine, and carries the same label as in usitc/hts and census/schedule_b.

Two forms of one code in one package. `ndc.code` is the NDC as claims carry it, digits only and padded to 5, 9 or 11 digits by level (labeler, product, package); `ndc.code_display` is the FDA's own hyphenated form, 4 or 5 digits for a labeler and up to 12 characters with its hyphens for a package. finetype's NDC pattern admits only the package forms of each, so each column declares the shapes it holds, and one shared pattern or length would be false of one of them.
